sources.title: Languages
notes: The federal administration serves the public in German, French and Italian, with some material in Romansh and English.
The German, French and Italian versions of federal laws are legally equivalent.
Language services reflect the needs of a multilingual population.

sources.title: Federal Act on the National Languages and Understanding between the Linguistic Communities
notes: German, French and Italian are federal official languages; Romansh is official in dealings with Romansh speakers.
The law aims to strengthen quadrilingualism and cohesion between language communities.
Federal authorities are directed to account for traditional regional language composition.

sources.title: What languages do Swiss people speak?
notes: Switzerland has four national languages: German, French, Italian and Romansh.
The country includes German-, French-, Italian- and Romansh-speaking regions.
Some cantons are bilingual and Graubünden is officially trilingual.

sources.title: French, German, Italian, Romansh, English: How do the Swiss talk to each other?
notes: Language boundaries are real but everyday language use is more intertwined than a simple map suggests.
German is the largest language group, followed by French and Italian, while Romansh is spoken by a small minority.
Migration and multilingualism influence language use.

sources.title: Switzerland: Country facts
sources.publisher: Federal Department of Finance, Swiss Confederation
notes: Switzerland has four language regions and 26 cantons.
German, French, Italian and Romansh are national languages.
Federalism and multilingualism are rooted in the country's history and continue to shape institutions.
